title: Opinion: This is Enric Mas’ time to shine, and boy is he
content:
Cyclist
Opinion: This is Enric Mas’ time to shine, and boy is he

One minute and 46 seconds. The closest margin between Enric Mas and victory throughout his career at the Vuelta a España, defeated at the hands of Simon Yates in 2018. The Spaniard’s fate at his home race has been perpetually intertwined with a palmarès of almosts – forever the bridesmaid at the final three-week race of the season.

It has never clicked for Mas in the other Grand Tours. In the Vuelta though, he comes alive. Three second places and one third means he’s more often been on the podium than off it in his seven Vuelta appearances. Following the unexpected abandonment of Tadej Pogačar though, this year he’s staring down the barrel of turning red jersey hopes into reality at long last.

The 2026 season has been subpar by Mas’s standards – and that of his Movistar team. Having entered the new year off the back of leg surgery, he clocked up some early kilometres in an uneventful Volta Ciclista a Catalunya before heading to Italy for the Giro d’Italia. Things didn’t go well. His own boss Eusebio Unzué admitted that the Giro was a ‘failure’ as Mas failed to leave his mark on the race, a second place on Stage 11 a consolation prize on his way to finishing 32nd overall. He would then miss the Tour de France for the first time since 2018.

A more positive indication of form arrived at the Vuelta a Burgos in August when multiple top finishes across the stages resulted in a fifth place overall on GC. As he approached the Vuelta a España, things were looking better for witnessing a typical Mas performance here. That no matter how the past few months had unfolded on the bike, once the final Grand Tour rolled around, he could salvage a decent result to carry into the dying embers of the season.

And so it began. Mas kept himself to the fore, riding onto the podium come the finale of Stage 4. Then the unthinkable happened on Stage 6, a day that saw Mas jump into second place – his consistency rewarded: he became one of only a handful of riders in recent history to follow an attack from Pogačar and reign in the seemingly untameable. Mas added his name to this short list with a blistering performance on the gravel of the Puerto El Bartolo. Catching and overhauling the race leader at the summit and snatching mountains points out of his rival’s hands, he even passed some advice to the World Champion on the descent. A universal gesture to slow down was not heeded by Pogačar, who then misjudged a corner and went off the road into the grass.  

Mas inherited the lead of the race following Pogačar’s abandonment on Stage 8. He refused to wear the red jersey on the podium at the end of the day, instead choosing to hold it as a sign of respect, then pulled it on the next morning to lead here for the first time in his career. He hasn’t put a pedal wrong so far, enjoying a resounding victory on Stage 9, and looks very comfortable as we delve further into this race. On Stage 12 with 11km remaining, he shrugged off his closest rivals of Primož Roglič and Felix Gall with ease. This is the best he’s ever looked.

There’s a certain feel to Mas at this Vuelta. Like a starving dog who finally gets its jaws around a scrap of food, he is ferociously baring his teeth at anyone who dares think about taking the red jersey from his clutches. This is his moment, and lord help anyone that gets in his way.

It should be noted as well that his Movistar teammates have stepped up too. While the UAE Team Emirates XRG GC stranglehold has dissipated to individual stage-hunting opportunities, Movistar deployed Raúl García Pierna today as a satellite rider in a show of tactical excellence to inflate Mas’ advantage by another half a minute over Roglič.  

As far as others waiting in the wings go, having someone that has amassed four red jerseys to their name in second might not be the most comforting prospect to some. Roglič is 1min 45sec back and only needs one more Vuelta victory to hold the record of most wins outright, but this has not been a shining season for him either and his inability to follow Mas already is unlikely to have the trophy engraver pause anytime soon. What does work in his favour is his almost laissez faire approach surrounding this Vuelta. Not a resignation – far from it – rather a chipping away at the days until he can potentially find some steam in the third week and embrace another time-trial. Then the Jaws music might play and Roglič might feast.

Gall is third overall and sits 2min 06sec down. Decathlon CMA CGM attempted to set up their main man on the road to Calar Alto, however it eventually came to nothing as he was forced to watch Mas ride away in the distance. That’s not to say there won’t come a day when the odds turn in their favour. All it takes is one crack here, a bonk there and a GC can turn on its head. The gap is not insurmountable.

But for now, at least, the standout performance on Stage 12 shows Mas is comfortable enough to launch a scathing offensive and indicates he has full control of the GC reins – even if he admitted to ‘not knowing’ the route that lies ahead. Maybe he just likes a surprise. This Grand Tour has certainly been full of them already.
